source.title: Festinger's Principle (the 90/10 rule) and Leon Festinger's big ideas
source.attribution: Summary in our own words of the popular "Festinger's Principle" (the 90/10 rule) and of Leon Festinger's research on social comparison (1954), When Prophecy Fails (1956) and cognitive dissonance (1957). Not affiliated with or endorsed by his estate or publishers.
source.notes: Original summary written by Reborn; contains no text from Festinger's books or papers, which are in copyright. The 90/10 rule is widely credited to Festinger online, but no source in his published work has been found; it is best known from Stephen Covey. Cards say so plainly and treat it as a popular principle, not as Festinger's research.

cards.title: 10% of life is what happens to you; 90% is how you react
cards.body:
Festinger's Principle, also called the 90/10 rule, splits life into two parts. About a tenth is made of events you can't control: the weather, a cancelled train, a careless word from someone else. The other nine tenths is decided by how you respond to them.

The numbers aren't meant as measurement. They make one point hard to forget: you rarely choose what happens, but you nearly always choose your next move, and that move shapes most of what follows.
cards.apply_it: The next time something goes wrong today, say quietly to yourself: "That's the 10%. What's my 90%?" Then pick your response on purpose.

quiz.question: What does the 90 in the 90/10 rule stand for?
quiz.explanation: The 10% is what happens to you; the 90% is your reaction, which you can shape.

cards.title: The spilled coffee: how one small accident can ruin a whole day
cards.body:
The principle is usually told as a story. At breakfast a child knocks over a cup and coffee soaks a father's work shirt. He shouts. She cries, rushes, and misses her school bus. He has to drive her, so he races and gets a speeding fine. He arrives late at work, still angry, snaps at a colleague, and comes home to a cold, tense house.

The spill took two seconds. Everything that went wrong after it came from the shouting, not from the coffee.
cards.apply_it: Think of your last really bad day. Find the first small event, then trace which later problems came from the event and which came from your reaction.

quiz.question: In the coffee story, what caused most of the bad day?
quiz.explanation: The spill was the 10%. The shouting set off the chain that ruined the day.

cards.title: Same spill, calm reaction, completely different day
cards.body:
Now replay the morning. The coffee spills. The father takes a breath and says, "It's fine, love, just be more careful next time." He goes upstairs and changes his shirt. His daughter catches her bus and waves from the window. He leaves on time, drives calmly, and starts work in a good mood.

The event was identical. The shirt was just as wet. The only thing that changed was a five-second choice, and that choice decided the next twelve hours.
cards.apply_it: Pick one small irritation you expect tomorrow, such as traffic or a slow colleague, and decide now the calm sentence you'll say when it happens.

quiz.question: What changed between the two versions of the coffee story?
quiz.explanation: The accident was the same. A calm response kept it a small event.

cards.title: Bad reactions spread like falling dominoes
cards.body:
A reaction is never the end of a moment. It becomes the next event that other people react to. Your sharp word makes someone defensive; their defensiveness makes you sharper; soon two people are having a bad day over something tiny.

The 90/10 rule asks you to see that chain before it starts. The first domino is often out of your hands, but you are usually the one who pushes the second. Stop there and the rest never fall.
cards.apply_it: When you feel a reaction rising, ask: "If I do this, what will they do next?" Let that picture slow you down.

quiz.question: Why does the 90/10 rule focus on your first reaction?
options: It is the only thing others notice
It often starts a chain of further events
It can undo the original event
quiz.explanation: Your reaction becomes the next event, so it sets off what follows.

cards.title: Win the gap between what happens and what you do
cards.body:
Between an event and your response there is a short gap. On a bad day it lasts half a second and you fill it with habit: a slammed door, a sarcastic reply, a honk of the horn. With practice, you can stretch that gap to a few seconds.

A few seconds is enough. It's enough to breathe out, notice the feeling, and ask what you actually want to happen next. Most regretted reactions happen because the gap was never used.
cards.apply_it: Practise a three-second pause today: when something annoys you, breathe out slowly before you speak or act.

quiz.question: What does the rule suggest you do with the gap before reacting?
options: Stretch it and choose your response
quiz.explanation: A short pause turns an automatic reaction into a chosen response.

cards.title: Stop spending energy on the 10% you can't change
cards.body:
Much of our frustration goes on events that are already over. The flight is delayed; the exam result is in; the rain has started. Replaying it, complaining about it, or wishing it were different changes nothing about the event, yet it drains the energy you need for the part you can change.

The 90/10 rule is a sorting tool. Put what happened in one pile and your options in another. Then spend your effort only on the second pile.
cards.apply_it: Write down something bothering you. Draw a line under it, and list three things you can still do about it. Act on one.

quiz.question: According to the rule, where should your energy go?
options: The responses still open to you
quiz.explanation: The event is fixed; your options are where effort still pays.

cards.title: Choosing your reaction doesn't mean pretending you feel fine
cards.body:
The 90/10 rule is sometimes misread as "never get upset". That's not it. Feeling annoyed when coffee ruins your shirt, or hurt when a friend lets you down, is normal and honest.

The choice is about what you do with the feeling. You can feel angry and still speak calmly. You can feel disappointed and still say clearly what you need. Naming the feeling, even just to yourself, often takes away much of its push.
cards.apply_it: Next time you're upset, name the feeling in one word ("frustrated", "embarrassed") before deciding what to do.

quiz.question: What does the 90/10 rule NOT ask you to do?
quiz.explanation: Feelings are fine; the rule is about the actions that follow them.

cards.title: Traffic, queues and delays: the 90/10 rule in daily life
cards.body:
Someone cuts in front of you on the road. You can chase them, flash your lights and arrive tense, or you can let them go and keep your morning. A shop queue is slow. You can sigh loudly, or use the minutes to rest your mind.

These moments seem too small to matter, but they come many times a day. Handled badly, they add up to a stressed, short-tempered person. Handled well, they add up to someone others find easy to be around.
cards.apply_it: Choose one daily annoyance, like the commute or a queue, and plan something useful to do in it, such as a podcast or a few slow breaths.

quiz.question: Why do small daily reactions matter so much?
options: They happen many times and add up
quiz.explanation: Small moments repeat all day, so their total effect is large.

cards.title: When someone criticises you, the criticism is the 10%
cards.body:
Harsh feedback lands like spilled coffee: sudden and unwelcome. The usual reactions are to argue, to sulk, or to quietly decide the person is against you. Each of those turns a single comment into a lasting problem.

A 90/10 response is simpler. Thank them, ask one question to understand it, and decide later, when you're calm, how much of it is true. Even unfair criticism loses most of its power when you don't let it steer your next move.
cards.apply_it: Next time you get criticism, reply only with "Thanks, can you give me an example?" and wait a day before deciding what you think.

quiz.question: What is a 90/10 way to handle criticism?
options: Ignore the person from now on
Ask a question and judge it later when calm
quiz.explanation: Calm curiosity keeps one comment from becoming a lasting conflict.

cards.title: Blame explains the 10%; responsibility owns the 90%
cards.body:
When things go wrong it's natural to look for someone to blame. Sometimes blame is accurate: the other driver really did cause the crash. But blame only answers "why did this happen?" It doesn't answer "what now?"

Taking responsibility doesn't mean accepting fault. It means accepting that the next step is yours. People who recover quickly from setbacks tend to move from the first question to the second sooner than most.
cards.apply_it: Think of a current problem someone else caused. Write one sentence about what you will do next, without mentioning them.

quiz.question: What does taking responsibility mean under the 90/10 rule?
options: Owning your next step, whoever was at fault
quiz.explanation: Fault and responsibility differ: the next move is yours either way.

cards.title: Good reactions are a habit you can train
cards.body:
Nobody masters the 90/10 rule by deciding to. Under pressure you fall back on habit, so the work is to build better habits before the pressure comes.

A few practices help: decide in advance how you'll handle common irritations; notice your early warning signs, like a tight jaw or a raised voice; and review the day each evening, asking where you reacted well and where you didn't. Each calm response makes the next one a little easier.
cards.apply_it: Tonight, recall one moment you reacted badly today. Replay it in your mind with the response you wish you'd chosen.

quiz.question: How does the rule become automatic?
options: By deciding once to be calm
By training better habits ahead of time
By waiting until you are older
quiz.explanation: Under pressure we fall back on habit, so practise the habit before you need it.

cards.title: Did Festinger really say it? An honest note on the 90/10 rule
cards.body:
Online, the 90/10 rule is almost always called Festinger's Principle, after the American psychologist Leon Festinger. Yet no one has traced it to anything he wrote or said. His research was about how people handle clashing beliefs and how they compare themselves with others, not about this rule.

The idea is best known from Stephen Covey, the author of The 7 Habits of Highly Effective People, who taught it widely. It is a useful principle whoever coined it. It's just worth knowing where it really comes from.
cards.apply_it: Next time a quote or rule is credited to a famous name, spend one minute searching where it first appeared before you repeat it.

quiz.question: Who is the 90/10 rule best known from?
quiz.explanation: It is credited to Festinger online, but it is best known from Stephen Covey's teaching.

cards.title: Cognitive dissonance: the discomfort of holding two clashing thoughts
cards.body:
Leon Festinger's best-known idea is that people feel real discomfort when two of their thoughts don't fit together, such as "I care about my health" and "I smoke". He called this tension cognitive dissonance.

Because it feels bad, we work to make it go away. We can change what we do, change what we believe, or add new thoughts that soften the clash ("my grandad smoked and lived to ninety"). Much of what looks like stubbornness is the mind easing this discomfort.
cards.apply_it: Think of one habit that doesn't match a value you hold. Notice which excuse you usually use to make the clash feel smaller.

quiz.question: What is cognitive dissonance?
quiz.explanation: Festinger described it as the tension felt when beliefs or actions don't fit together.

cards.title: Three ways the mind removes dissonance, and only one is change
cards.body:
Festinger saw that when actions and beliefs clash, people have three main options. They can change the action: stop smoking. They can change the belief: decide smoking isn't that harmful. Or they can add comforting thoughts: "it helps my stress", "everyone dies of something".

Changing the action is usually hardest, so the mind often picks one of the easier routes. Knowing this lets you catch yourself rewriting a belief just to avoid changing a habit.
cards.apply_it: When you hear yourself make an excuse, ask: "Am I changing my belief here because changing my behaviour is harder?"

quiz.question: Which way of reducing dissonance is often the hardest?
quiz.explanation: Because changing what we do takes effort, the mind often adjusts beliefs instead.

cards.title: The one-dollar experiment: why small rewards change minds more
cards.body:
In 1959 Festinger and James Carlsmith gave students an hour of dull tasks, like turning pegs on a board. Then they paid some students one dollar and others twenty dollars to tell the next participant the tasks were fun.

Later, the one-dollar group rated the tasks as more enjoyable. Twenty dollars was a good reason to fib, so no dissonance. One dollar wasn't, so those students eased the clash by half believing what they'd said.
cards.apply_it: Notice where you justify something you do with "I actually like it". Ask whether you'd still say so if nothing pushed you to do it.

quiz.question: In Festinger and Carlsmith's study, who later liked the dull task more?
quiz.explanation: With too little reward to justify the lie, the $1 group shifted their belief instead.

cards.title: After a hard choice, we talk up what we chose
cards.body:
Dissonance theory predicts that once you make a difficult decision, the good points of the option you turned down start to nag at you. To quiet them, people tend to rate their chosen option even higher afterwards, and the rejected one lower.

This is why buyers praise the car they just bought and spot faults in the one they nearly picked. It helps us move on, but it also makes it hard to admit when a choice was genuinely wrong.
cards.apply_it: Think of a recent big decision. Write down honestly one real strength of the option you didn't pick.

quiz.question: What do people often do after making a hard choice?
options: Rate the chosen option higher than before
Ask others to decide next time
quiz.explanation: Talking up the choice reduces the dissonance of having given up a good alternative.

cards.title: The harder we work for something, the more we value it
cards.body:
If you suffer to get something and it turns out to be dull, you have a clash: "I worked hard for this" and "this isn't worth much". It's easier to decide it is worth a lot.

Researchers building on Festinger's theory showed that people who went through an embarrassing test to join a group rated the group's boring discussion as more interesting. This helps explain loyalty to tough clubs, costly courses and hard-won goals.
cards.apply_it: Pick something you value partly because it was hard to get. Ask whether you'd choose it again if it were easy.

quiz.question: Why might a hard entry test make people like a group more?
options: Valuing the group justifies the effort
quiz.explanation: Liking the group eases the clash between high effort and a low reward.

cards.title: We avoid information that could unsettle our beliefs
cards.body:
Festinger predicted that people would seek out information that supports what they already think and steer away from information that challenges it, because challenging facts bring dissonance.

You can see it in the news people choose, the friends they follow and the articles they skip. The result is a comfortable bubble that feels like knowledge. Thinking well means sometimes choosing the uncomfortable article on purpose.
cards.apply_it: This week, read one thoughtful piece that argues against a view you hold. Note one point you find fair.

quiz.question: According to dissonance theory, what information do people tend to avoid?
quiz.explanation: Challenging information creates discomfort, so people often steer away from it.

cards.title: When Prophecy Fails: why some beliefs grow stronger after being disproved
cards.body:
In 1954 Festinger and two colleagues joined a small group in the United States whose leader said a great flood would end the world on 21 December, and believers would be rescued by spacecraft. Members quit jobs and gave away belongings.

The date passed. Nothing happened. Many didn't give up the belief. Instead they decided their faith had saved the world, and began trying to win new followers, something they had avoided before.
cards.apply_it: Think of a time you held on to a plan or belief after evidence went against it. What made letting go so hard?

quiz.question: What did many members do after the predicted flood didn't happen?
options: Believed more and sought new followers
quiz.explanation: Having given up so much, many reduced dissonance by believing harder and recruiting others.

cards.title: The more you've invested in a belief, the harder it is to drop
cards.body:
When Prophecy Fails set out the conditions for this doubling down. The belief is deeply held; the person has acted on it in ways hard to undo; the belief is clearly disproved; and there are fellow believers for support.

The same pattern shows up far from doomsday groups: investors holding a falling share, managers defending a failing project, partners staying in a relationship that has ended in all but name. The bigger the investment, the stronger the pull to explain away the evidence.
cards.apply_it: List one thing you keep defending mainly because of what you've already put into it. Ask: "If I were starting fresh today, would I choose this?"

quiz.question: Which condition makes doubling down on a failed belief more likely?
options: Being alone with no fellow believers
Having taken big, hard-to-undo actions for it
quiz.explanation: Large, irreversible commitments make admitting the error feel too costly.

cards.title: Use dissonance for good: act first, and your beliefs will follow
cards.body:
Dissonance usually gets blamed for excuses, but it can work for you. Because people like their actions and beliefs to match, small actions can pull beliefs along behind them.

If you go for a short run three mornings in a row, "I'm not a runner" starts to clash with what you're doing, and your mind starts to see you as someone who runs. Small, freely chosen actions work best, because you can't explain them away as forced.
cards.apply_it: Choose a habit you want and do a tiny version of it today, so small it's easy. Repeat it tomorrow and notice how you start to describe yourself.

quiz.question: How can dissonance help build a habit?
options: Small actions shift beliefs about who you are
By thinking about the habit without acting
quiz.explanation: When actions change, beliefs tend to shift to match them.

cards.title: How to spot dissonance in yourself
cards.body:
Dissonance is hard to see from the inside because the mind smooths it over quickly. A few signs give it away: you feel oddly defensive about a small choice; you reach for an excuse before anyone has asked; you avoid looking at a bank balance, a scale or a message; or you are suddenly sure that the people who disagree are foolish.

None of these mean you're wrong. They mean there's a clash worth looking at calmly.
cards.apply_it: Next time you feel defensive, stop and finish this sentence: "The thing I don't want to admit is..."

quiz.question: Which is a sign you may be easing dissonance?
options: Feeling defensive before anyone challenges you
quiz.explanation: Rushing to defend yourself is a common sign of a clash being smoothed over.

cards.title: Why facts alone rarely change someone's mind
cards.body:
Dissonance theory explains why piling on evidence often fails. To accept your facts, the other person must admit they were wrong, and that clashes with "I'm a sensible person". The easiest way out is to doubt you, not themselves.

People change their minds more easily when they can keep their self-respect. Ask questions instead of lecturing, agree with what's fair in their view, and leave them room to change their mind later, in private.
cards.apply_it: In your next disagreement, start by saying one thing the other person is right about before you share your view.

quiz.question: Why do facts alone often fail to persuade?
options: Accepting them means admitting a mistake, which feels threatening
quiz.explanation: Changing your mind clashes with seeing yourself as sensible, so people resist.

cards.title: Social comparison: we judge ourselves by looking at others
cards.body:
In 1954 Festinger argued that people have a basic drive to know how they're doing: how able they are, whether their opinions are right. When there's no clear, objective measure, we judge ourselves by comparing with other people.

He added that we prefer to compare with people who are fairly similar to us. A beginner runner learns little from an Olympic champion, but a lot from someone who started a few months earlier.
cards.apply_it: Pick one skill you're working on and find someone just a little ahead of you. Ask them what helped them most.
cards.locator: A Theory of Social Comparison Processes (1954)

quiz.question: According to Festinger, when do people compare themselves with others most?
options: When a clear objective measure exists
When there's no clear objective measure
quiz.explanation: Without an objective yardstick, other people become the yardstick.

cards.title: Social media turns comparison into a full-time job
cards.body:
Festinger described comparison long before social media, but the feed puts his idea on overdrive. We see other people's best moments, chosen and polished, and set them against our ordinary days.

Later researchers found that comparing upwards can inspire us when the gap feels reachable, and crush us when it doesn't. Scrolling past hundreds of perfect lives a day pushes most of us towards the crushing kind.
cards.apply_it: Check how you feel after ten minutes on social media. If it's worse, mute the accounts that leave you feeling small.
cards.locator: A Theory of Social Comparison Processes (1954)

quiz.question: When does upward comparison tend to inspire rather than discourage?
options: When the other person is famous
When you compare many times a day
quiz.explanation: A reachable gap motivates; an impossible one deflates.

cards.title: Compare yourself with who you were, not with who they are
cards.body:
Since comparison is a deep human drive, trying never to compare rarely works. A better move is to choose your comparisons. The fairest one is with your own past: what you could do, know or handle a year ago.

This kind of comparison measures real progress, uses the same starting point and the same circumstances, and leaves room for pride without anyone having to lose.
cards.apply_it: Write down three things you can do now that you couldn't do a year ago.
cards.locator: A Theory of Social Comparison Processes (1954)

quiz.question: What is the fairest comparison for tracking your growth?
quiz.explanation: Your past self shares your circumstances, so the comparison shows real progress.

cards.title: Groups pull their members' opinions together
cards.body:
Festinger noticed that people in a group feel pressure to agree, because others' opinions are how we check our own. When someone disagrees, the group talks to them most, trying to bring them round. If that fails, the group may quietly stop treating them as one of its own.

This helps explain why friends drift towards the same views, and why it takes courage to be the one who disagrees in a meeting.
cards.apply_it: In your next group discussion, notice whether anyone holds back a different view. Invite it: "Does anyone see this differently?"

quiz.question: What did Festinger say groups do with a member who disagrees?
options: Communicate with them most to bring them round
Change the group's view at once
quiz.explanation: Pressure to agree shows up as more talk aimed at the person who differs.

cards.title: Leon Festinger: the psychologist who studied how we fool ourselves
cards.body:
Leon Festinger was born in New York City in 1919 to a family of Russian Jewish immigrants. He studied under Kurt Lewin, a founder of social psychology, and went on to teach at MIT, Michigan, Minnesota, Stanford and the New School in New York. He died in 1989.

He is often ranked among the most influential psychologists of the 20th century. His gift was turning everyday puzzles, like why we make excuses, into clear theories and clever experiments.
cards.apply_it: Choose one everyday puzzle about people that bugs you. Write down a simple experiment that might test your best guess about it.

quiz.question: Which famous psychologist was Festinger's teacher?
quiz.explanation: Festinger studied under Kurt Lewin, a founder of social psychology.

cards.title: Friendships grow from who you happen to pass every day
cards.body:
In a 1950 study of a student housing estate called Westgate, Festinger and his colleagues asked residents who their closest friends were. Distance turned out to matter enormously: people were far more likely to befriend next-door neighbours than those a few doors away. Residents whose doors faced the stairs or the mailboxes made the most friends.

Friendship often starts with simple, repeated contact. Being where people naturally pass gives it a chance to begin.
cards.apply_it: Choose one place you could show up regularly, like a class, a club or a café, and go three times in the next fortnight.

quiz.question: What best predicted friendships in the Westgate study?
quiz.explanation: Living close and crossing paths often made friendships far more likely.

cards.title: Festinger kept switching fields to stay curious
cards.body:
At the height of his fame, Festinger surprised colleagues by leaving social psychology. He spent years studying how the eye and brain see, then turned to archaeology and history, asking how humans developed from early tool makers into complex societies. He wrote a book about this, The Human Legacy, in 1983.

He said he moved on when he felt a field had stopped surprising him. His career is a reminder that curiosity can outlast expertise.
cards.apply_it: Pick a subject far from your work that you're curious about, and spend twenty minutes this week learning its basics.

quiz.question: What did Festinger turn to after social psychology?
quiz.explanation: He studied vision and later human prehistory, writing The Human Legacy.

cards.title: Bold predictions make a theory worth testing
cards.body:
Festinger liked theories that made surprising, risky predictions. Common sense said a bigger reward would change attitudes more; dissonance theory said a smaller one would, and his experiments backed it. Common sense said a failed prophecy would end a belief; his theory said it might strengthen it.

A claim that could never be shown wrong teaches little. A clear prediction that might fail, and then doesn't, is what makes a good idea convincing.
cards.apply_it: Next time you hold a strong opinion, write down what result would prove you wrong. If nothing could, question the opinion.

quiz.question: What made Festinger's theories persuasive?
options: They made risky predictions that held up
quiz.explanation: Surprising predictions that survive testing are strong evidence.

cards.title: The 90/10 rule and dissonance meet in your excuses
cards.body:
Put the two ideas together and a pattern appears. After a bad reaction, the shouting at breakfast, say, we feel dissonance: "I'm a good parent" clashes with "I made my child cry over coffee". The easy fix is an excuse: she should have been more careful; I was stressed.

The excuse soothes us but blocks learning. The honest fix is harder and better: admit the reaction was the problem, apologise, and plan a better one next time.
cards.apply_it: Think of a recent reaction you regret. Instead of an excuse, write one sentence of apology and one sentence of what you'll do differently.

quiz.question: What does an excuse do after a bad reaction?
options: Eases the discomfort but blocks learning
quiz.explanation: Excuses reduce dissonance cheaply, so we skip the lesson.

cards.title: When you get the 90% wrong, the repair is part of the 90%
cards.body:
Nobody reacts well every time. The spilled coffee will sometimes win and you'll snap. The 90/10 rule still applies: the bad reaction is now the event, and your next response is the new choice.

A quick, sincere repair, such as "I'm sorry I shouted, the shirt doesn't matter, you do", can stop the chain of bad events halfway. It also teaches the people around you that mistakes can be fixed.
cards.apply_it: If you snapped at someone recently, go back today and say a simple sorry, without adding "but".

quiz.question: What should you do after reacting badly, according to the rule?
options: Treat it as the new event and choose a repair
Wait for the other person to apologise
quiz.explanation: Your bad reaction becomes the next 10%; a repair is your next 90%.

cards.title: A one-minute recap: control the controllable, and be honest with yourself
cards.body:
Two lessons run through these cards. From the popular 90/10 rule: you can't control most of what happens, but you can choose most of what comes next, and small choices shape whole days. From Leon Festinger's real research: the mind hates inner contradiction and will bend beliefs, memories and excuses to avoid it.

The practice joins them. Pause before reacting, then look honestly at what you did, without the comforting stories.
cards.apply_it: Set a reminder for this evening that says "10% or 90%?" and use it to review one moment from your day.

quiz.question: Which pair of ideas do these cards combine?
quiz.explanation: The popular 90/10 rule plus Festinger's dissonance research.
